Accessibility

You might say

I heard some people browse without a mouse, using a screen reader—check whether they can use this page properly.

Accessibility means more people can use your page in more situations—not only with a mouse, not only with perfect vision, and even read aloud by a screen reader.·You test with a mouse and good eyes, but visitors may use a keyboard, a screen reader, or squint at a phone in sunlight. Accessibility extends "works for me" to those situations: text alternatives on images, buttons reachable by Tab, sufficient text contrast. When an AI reply mentions a11y, it is the shorthand for this word (a plus 11 letters plus y).
Know first

Portfolio example screenshot
alt'Portfolio example: project background, process, results'
Good accessibility benefits everyonea11y = a + 11 letters + y, common in AI replies.
Three high-frequency checks

Images have text alternatives: Every informative image carries alt text that steps in when the image fails or a reader reads aloud. Purely decorative icons can go without it—just do not skip images with content.

Keyboard can reach: Unplug the mouse and Tab through: every button reachable, focus visible (the focus ring), order sensible. Menus and dialogs take focus in and return it on close.

Contrast suffices: Body versus background at least 4.5:1. This one also helps everyone squinting at a phone in the sun—good accessibility benefits ordinary users too.

What it is not

Accessibility is not only "helping people with disabilities"—sunlight glare, holding a baby with one hand, or a broken mouse all fall inside it, and everyone benefits. It is also not a post-launch patch: doing these checks during the build is straightforward; auditing every page after launch takes far more time. The a11y shorthand common in AI replies refers to exactly this.

Run an accessibility self-check before delivery: every image has alt text, all buttons and links are reachable by Tab in order, and body contrast is at least 4.5:1. Fix what fails and list the fixes.
